nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body: June 15, 1993.  T.D. Philipps; Mote Marine Laboratory

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Scientific Name: Sphyrna tiburo
Common Name:  Bonnethead shark

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class: Elasmobranchiomorphi
      Order: Lamniformes
      Family: Sphyrnidae

Other Common Names:  Bonnetnose (312 327), shovel-nose shark (312 581), bonnet-headed (8341, bonnet shark, shovel head (52).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  No regular fishery exists (791) and of no commercial value and little economic value (52 101). Occasionally marketed fresh or salted (52 791).

Recreational: Commonly caught from bridges (788) and said to be lively sport on light tackle (101).

nodes.title: Indicator
nodes.body: Ecological Role: Sometimes a prey for other shark species (791).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body: Overall:  Western Atlantic from Massachusetts (occasional) throughout the Caribbean to Brazil and northern Argentina (101 327 788). Absent from the islands except Cuba and the western Bahamas (788). In the eastern Pacific from southern California to Ecuador (52 101).

nodes.title: By State
nodes.body:
Within Study Area: Common throughout Florida waters.

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: Nektonic, often occurring in schools in shallow coastal waters of 10-25 m depth but found out to 80 m (327 791). Common in river estuaries and around coral reefs (791). Schools usually are made up of 5-15 individuals (101) but large schools containing as many as 700 individuals have been reported (865).

nodes.title: Movements/Migrations
nodes.body: In Florida it is believed that there is a southern movement in winter or that there is a migration to deeper water in winter (101). Parsons (863) reported an average swimming velocity of 41 cm/second.

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Chiefly in shallow water close inshore and often in bays and estuaries (52).  In Louisiana they are also found in the saltier bays (327).

Substrate: Reported from both sand and muddy bottoms (101 791).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body: Juvenile/adults: At Cedar Key, Florida, collected at temperatures from 28.9 to 30.60 C (581). In Charlotte Harbor, from 25 to 310 C (789).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body: Juvenile/adults: Collected from 25.6 to 29 % at Cedar Key (581) and from 19.5 to 35.5 % in Charlotte Harbor (789).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body: Reproductive Mode: Fertilization is internal and reproduction is viviparous.

nodes.title: Mating/Spawning
nodes.body:
Maturity is said to occur at a size between 107 and 122 cm (52), but in southwest Florida, Clark and von Schmidt (123) reported a mature female of 87 cm and stated that males mature at 76 cm and larger.

Fecundity: Fecundity estimates range from 6 to 12 embryos per female (52 101 791 834). One study found females to have as many as 12 to 14 embryos or uterine eggs (123).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body: Juveniles/Adults: Maximum size has been reported as 150 cm (788 791). Bigelow and Schroeder (52) stated that ?few grow longer than 5 feet M (152 cm).

nodes.title: Food Items
nodes.body: Diet is primarily crustaceans including crabs and shrimp (101 327 788 834). Two studies specifically mention blue crabs (123 255). They are frequently caught by fishermen using shrimp for bait (123). Other food items include clams, octopus, isopods, and small fish (52 101 123 791).
